newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House supports further NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House supports further NATO expansion.

text.p: The U.S House of Representatives voted on Wednesday to support expansion of NATO and designated Romania and the Baltic States as eligible for U.S. assistance in seeking membership.

While House International Relations Committee chairman Ben Gilman, Republican of New York, acknowledged that Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovenia are the frontrunners for NATO enlargement, he said the legislation would encourage further expansion.
It does not, however, bind the administration to any action in regards to next month's first round of talks on enlargement of the Atlantic alliance.
A bipartisan group of senators told President Bill Clinton during a meeting on Wednesday that U.S. Senate approval of NAT0 expansion would not be automatic.

"No foreign policy, no matter how well thought out, can be sustained without the informed support of the American people. Now is the time to inform them," said Democratic Sen. Joseph Biden of Delaware.
Biden, who serves on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said some of his colleagues expressed scepticism about NATO enlargement at the White House meeting "but there was no outright opposition."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and National Security Adviser Samuel Berger also took part in the meeting.

The House measure passed on a voice vote immediately after the House also approved a separate bill calling for reorganization of the State Department and reauthorizing its programmes for another year.
"We are concerned about the countries that may be left out of the first round of enlargement. It is critical that such countries not be left in any security vacuum," Gilman said.
"This bill reassures these countries that they will not be forgotten: that the door to NATO will remain open to them," he said.
In France on Tuesday, European centrist leaders including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl called for Romania to be included in the first wave for membership in 1999.
NATO is due to annouce at a summit in Madrid on July 8 and 9 the names of the first countries from eastern Europe that will be invited to begin negotiations for membership in 1999.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are widely tipped to be the frontrunners, with Slovenia and Romania often mentioned as outside chances.
In approving the State Department bill, the House agreed to a provision placing abortion-related restrictions on U.S. family planning aid to international groups.

The bill called for reorganization of the State Department by bringing two foreign affairs agencies, the U.S. Information Agency and the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and parts of the Agency for International Development into the State Department.

The White House has said it could not accept the detailed structure of the reorganization set out in the House bill, though the administration has started work on a consolidation plan for its foreign affairs agencies.
